                             REQUESTS FOR REHEARING

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”),1 Tennessee Gas Pipeline Company, L.L.C.

(“TGP”), Southern Natural Gas Company, L.L.C. (“SNG”), and Elba Express Company, L.L.C.

(“EEC” and, together with TGP and SNG, the “Companies”) hereby submit this response

(“Answer”) to the request for rehearing and motion for stay filed in these proceedings by anti-

infrastructure organizations and landowners (collectively, the “Anti-Infrastructure Groups”)

opposing the Commission’s Order Issuing Certificates and Approving Abandonment for the

Mississippi Crossing Project proposed by TGP (“MSX”) and the South System Expansion 4 Project

proposed by SNG and EEC (“SSE4” and, together with MSX, the “Projects”).2 The Companies

Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, and also landowners Mary Avery, Carl Moseley, and Kenny Owen
(the “Landowners”).

 also hereby respond to the request for rehearing filed by landowner John Peek (the “Peek Rehearing

Request”).3

          The Companies are entitled to answer the Motion for Stay under the Commission’s

generally applicable procedures.4          In addition, pursuant to Rules 212 and 213(a)(2) of the

Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,5 the Companies respectfully move for leave to

respond to the Rehearing Request and the Peek Rehearing Request. The Commission accepts

answers to rehearing requests for good cause—i.e., when they are likely to assist with its decision-

making process.6 This Answer will do just that by responding to the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’

material mischaracterization of the Projects, Commission and judicial precedent, and the record

established in these proceedings. The Commission should accept this Answer to ensure a complete

and accurate record that will aid the Commission’s decision-making.

I.        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

          The Rehearing Request filed by the Southern Environmental Law Center (“SELC”) on

behalf of the Anti-Infrastructure Groups runs over 300 pages, identifies 42 points of supposed error,

and appends more than 1,600 pages of attachments. Its length should not be mistaken for merit.

Judge Henderson of the D.C. Circuit recently described the strategy this kind of filing reflects: anti-

infrastructure groups “deluge permitting agencies with dubious claims” they need not even win

“because delay is the coin of the realm.”7 Disregarding the Commission’s direction to provide only

(“Peek Rehearing Request”).

delay through obfuscation.

          The Companies begin by addressing the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ motion for stay, which

the Commission should deny. To justify the extraordinary stay remedy, the Anti-Infrastructure

Groups face a heightened burden of demonstrating that the very same Projects the Commission just

recently determined to be required by the public convenience and necessity must now be subject

to indefinite delay. The Anti-Infrastructure Groups fail to meet their burden, and specifically

because they fail to establish irreparable harm. Instead, both the Landowners and the Anti-

Infrastructure Groups assert a variety of speculative harms that have also already been considered

by the Commission as part of its public interest determination underlying the Certificate Order.

Moreover, a stay would cause substantial harm to the Companies and their customers by delaying

the commencement of service on much-needed capacity that is designed to serve growing

residential, industrial, and commercial demand in a capacity-constrained region.              The

Commission’s public interest determination in the Certificate Order warrants prompt

commencement of service, not indefinite delay.

          The Companies next turn to the Anti-Infrastructure Group’s request for rehearing. As a

threshold matter, the Rehearing Request’s length, indiscriminate scope, and transparently improper

motivation are independently disqualifying. The Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ sprawling attack on

virtually every factfinding and legal conclusion in the Certificate Order serves neither of the

purposes rehearing exists to fulfill–correcting error or clarifying specific points—and is plainly

designed to make it as difficult as possible for the Commission to meaningfully engage with each

argument in the time Congress allotted.        The only reasonable inference is that the Anti-

                                                 3
 Infrastructure Groups are once again seeking to impose, through improper and procedurally

abusive means, the same expense and delay they have pursued throughout this proceeding in the

hope that if the Commission is sufficiently deluged, it will commit some minor foot fault at which

a court might look askance. The Commission should address and reject each of the Rehearing

Request’s arguments, but should deny the Rehearing Request on that independent, alternative

ground also.

        Next, the Companies take the opportunity to clarify what is, and is not, part of the record

before the Commission. The Anti-Infrastructure Groups repeatedly cite and re-attach materials the

Commission has already rejected as untimely or decried as having been filed out of time and for

improper purposes, together with more than 1,600 pages of entirely new materials introduced for

the first time in the Rehearing Request, and asks the Commission to treat all of it as established

record evidence. It is not, and the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ re-attachment of previously rejected

or newly introduced materials does not make it so. The Commission should disregard the Anti-

Infrastructure Groups’ reliance on these materials on the ground that the materials were never

properly filed in the first place.

        Turning to the substance, the great majority of the Rehearing Request does not even attempt

to identify any error in the Commission’s reasoning. It simply repeats arguments that the Anti-

Infrastructure Groups have already raised, and that the Commission and the Companies have

already addressed, repeatedly and thoroughly, at earlier stages of this multi-year proceeding. This

includes responses to the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ prior motions to lodge, environmental

comments, objections to the protective agreement, motion to compel, and previous motion to stay.

Rather than take the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ bait and needlessly re-answer positions the record

has already resolved, the Companies attach as Attachment A a table that maps several repeated

arguments in the Rehearing Request to the prior filing in which the Anti-Infrastructure Groups


                                                 4
 raised it and the specific paragraphs of the Certificate Order and the Companies’ prior answers that

already addressed it. While not exhaustive, and intended to be read in parallel with this Answer,

Attachment A is offered to assist the Commission in confirming, argument by argument, that the

bulk of the Rehearing Request may be denied on the existing record.

       The remainder of this Answer addresses several of the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’

arguments. First, the Companies explain why the Commission’s finding of project need remains

sound. The Certificate Order appropriately relied on binding precedent agreements covering

approximately 93% of the MSX Project’s capacity and 100% of the SSE4 Project’s capacity,

consistent with the D.C. Circuit’s recent confirmation that the Commission “may find market need

by relying solely on a precedent agreement” absent plausible evidence of self-dealing.9 The Anti-

Infrastructure Groups identify no such evidence here. Their arguments instead rest on rejected

litigation-driven market studies, an affiliate relationship of the sort that the Commission has

routinely found insufficient to establish self-dealing, and state-law fuel cost recovery issues with

no bearing on market need for the Projects.

       The Companies continue responding to the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ flawed Natural Gas

Act (“NGA”) analysis by addressing the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ contention that the

Commission’s benefit/harm balancing was arbitrary, and the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ renewed

reliance on state commission materials concerning an affiliate of a single Project’s customer.

Neither argument has merit.      The Commission’s balancing analysis satisfied the NGA by

identifying the Projects’ benefits and reasonably weighing them against the Projects’ adverse

effects, consistent with binding D.C. Circuit precedent and the Commission’s own recent orders;

 nothing in the law required the Commission to reduce those benefits to a single quantified figure.

And the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ captive-ratepayer theory rests entirely on materials the

Commission already excluded from the record, concerns a company that is not even a Project

customer, and flouts and mischaracterizes the D.C. Circuit’s decision in New Jersey Conservation

Foundation v. FERC.10

           Second, the Companies address the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ environmental arguments

and demonstrate that the Commission’s environmental review, including its analysis of cumulative

impacts, air quality, waterbody crossings, wetlands, the Natchez Trace Parkway and Big Black

River, threatened and endangered species, and pipeline safety, fully satisfied the Commission’s

obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) and the Endangered Species

Act (“ESA”).

           Third, and finally, the Companies respond to the Peek Rehearing Request, establishing that

it offers no basis on which the Commission should depart from its findings in the Certificate Order.

The Peek Rehearing Request impermissibly raises unsubstantiated allegations of impropriety for

the first time on rehearing and offers no basis for the Commission to reconsider its past rejection

of a proposed routing alternative.

           For these reasons, and for those discussed in detail below, the Commission should deny the

Motion for Stay, the Rehearing Request, and the Peek Rehearing Request in full.

II.        ANSWER TO MOTION FOR STAY

           The same Anti-Infrastructure Groups whose “eleventh-hour filing” the Commission

deemed to be “an inappropriate attempt to delay” Commission action11 now seek a stay of that very

 action. Like the Anti-Infrastructure Groups’ eleventh-hour filing (and the Anti-Infrastructure

Groups’ numerous other unsuccessful attempts to derail this proceeding by over-papering the

record with meritless arguments)12 the Motion for Stay (“Motion”) has no merit and should be

rejected.

        Under the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), the Commission may stay its action only

upon a finding that “justice so requires.”13 Accordingly, “[a] stay pending rehearing and judicial

review is an extraordinary remedy and is not a matter of right.”14 Consistent with that standard,

and reflecting the need “to assure definitiveness and finality in Commission proceedings,” “the

Commission’s longstanding policy” in the context of NGA section 7 authorizations “has been to

disfavor requests for stay.”15 In the application of that policy, the Commission considers: (1)

whether the moving party will suffer irreparable injury without a stay; (2) whether a stay would

substantially harm other parties, including the applicants; and (3) whether the stay is in the public

interest.16 If the moving party fails to demonstrate irreparable harm, the Commission need not

          Applying these factors and the longstanding policy disfavoring stays, the Commission

should deny the Motion.

          A.     The Motion Should Be Denied Because It Fails to Demonstrate Irreparable
                 Harm

          To satisfy the first requirement of “irreparable harm,” the asserted harm must be certain,

great, and actual.19 Bare allegations of what is merely likely to occur do not suffice.20 The party

seeking a stay has the burden of proving—not merely asserting—that the harm either (a) has

occurred in the past and is likely to occur again or (b) that the harm is certain to occur in the near

future.21 A stay “will not be granted against something merely feared as liable to occur at some

indefinite time” in the future.22 Moreover, the alleged injury must be “beyond remediation,” so

           The Anti-Infrastructure Groups cannot satisfy the first requirement for a stay—irreparable

harm—because their claims are speculative, unsupported by evidence, and largely a repackaging

of positions the Commission has already rejected.

                   1. The Motion Fails to Demonstrate that Landowners Would Suffer
                      Irreparable Harm Warranting a Stay

           As to the Landowners, the Motion fails to establish that any asserted harm resulting from

construction activities, easement acquisition, or eminent domain proceedings is irreparable.

Rather, the concerns they identify are largely speculative and, in any event, precisely the types of

issues that the Commission already considered and addressed when issuing the Certificate Order.

           Ms. Avery decries potential impacts on agricultural soils, timber, drainage patterns, farming

operations, and recreational uses of her property;25 Mr. Moseley complains of construction in

proximity to his septic system, fruit trees, utility infrastructure, and pet cemetery;26 and Mr. Owen

points to ongoing condemnation proceedings and hypothesizes potential effects on timber

resources, wildlife habitat, a lake, and access across his property.27 But there is nothing unusual,

much less extraordinary, about the proposition that interstate pipeline construction and operation

may have effects on private properties; that is why Congress expressly empowered certificate

 holders to exercise the eminent domain power.28           The Commission—aware of Congress’s

authorization—thus weighs such potential concerns as part of the certificate process. Here, the

Commission conducted that weighing and expressly concluded that the Projects were required by

the public convenience and necessity. There is no basis to perform the same analysis anew in the

context of a request for stay, particularly given that the considerations Landowners invoke are

subject to Commission-required mitigation and restoration measures.29

          Those measures—not a stay—are the appropriate means of addressing Landowners’ issues.

Among other things, the Companies must identify and avoid sensitive site-specific features where

practicable, coordinate with affected landowners regarding construction activities, comply with

detailed restoration requirements, and implement Commission-approved environmental mitigation

measures.30 Consistent with those requirements, the Companies have continued efforts to engage

with these landowners since the Certificate Order’s issuance. That ongoing engagement refutes

any claim that harm to a particular parcel is certain or imminent and instead demonstrates that site-

specific concerns are being actively addressed through the mitigation process the Certificate Order

requires. Far from preventing harm, a stay would disrupt that ongoing process.

                      Would Suffer Irreparable Harm in the Absence of a Stay

and irreparable injury necessary to support a stay. Much of the asserted harm consists of concerns

the Commission has already examined and addressed in the Certificate Order following a

          Alabama Rivers Alliance alleges that construction activities, particularly open-cut

trenching at certain waterbody crossings, could result in sedimentation and related impacts

by the Commission, FERC Staff fully considered these and other impacts, concluding that the

Projects’ impacts would not be significant.31 Thus, in issuing the Certificate Order for the Projects,

the Commission has already “carefully considered and balanced the alleged harms of the project[s]

against [their] benefits.”32

          Blackbelt Women Rising (“BBWR”) likewise fails to identify any concrete injury

warranting a stay. It asserts that construction may burden Black Belt communities and require the

organization to devote resources toward community outreach, education, and advocacy relating to

the Projects. But any such injury is speculative and self-inflicted, and the Commission has

expressly held that “time and energy necessarily expended in the absence of a stay are not enough”

to demonstrate irreparable harm.33 BBWR’s allegations of harm thus rest on speculation and self-

           Energy Alabama fares no better. It contends that construction of the Projects will further

long-term reliance on natural gas infrastructure, hinder its efforts to advocate for alternative energy

resources, and require additional advocacy concerning potential future ratepayer exposure to fuel

costs. But these assertions depend on a chain of assumptions concerning future energy markets,

resource-planning decisions, and policy developments extending well beyond construction of the

Projects. Such generalized policy objections and predictions about future market conditions are

far removed from the type of concrete and immediate injury required to support a stay.35 Further,

to the extent Energy Alabama claims it will incur additional advocacy or outreach costs, those

expenditures likewise reflect the organization’s own decisions regarding how to pursue its mission,

not an imminent and irreparable injury caused by the Projects. Moreover, issues concerning state-

regulated retail rates, in addition to being highly speculative, fall outside of the Commission’s

purview and jurisdiction in this NGA section 7 proceeding.

           In sum, the Anti-Infrastructure Groups have failed to carry their burden of establishing

irreparable harm. Their allegations rest on speculation, policy disagreements, and self-directed

organizational choices rather than any concrete injury that is certain and imminent. As the

Commission has recognized, “bare allegations of what is likely to occur” do not suffice.36 Because

           B.      The Motion Should Be Denied Because a Stay Would Substantially Harm the
                   Companies, and the Motion Fails to Establish Otherwise
